meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Answer to the Great Question of Life, the Universe and Everything is Forty-two'?
meta.ogDescription: Real quote. Deep Thought delivers it in chapter 27 of Douglas Adams's 1979 novel — the answer first aired on BBC Radio 4 on 29 March 1978.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and easy to check. The supercomputer Deep Thought delivers it in Chapter 27 of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, first published in London by Pan Books on 12 October 1979 ↗; the answer had already reached the public on BBC Radio 4 in “Fit the Fourth” on 29 March 1978. The book sets the line out with Adams’s own pauses — “The Answer to the Great Question… Of Life, the Universe and Everything… Is… Forty-two” — which the popular one-line form smooths away.

source.excerpt: “All right,” said Deep Thought. “The Answer to the Great Question…” […] “Of Life, the Universe and Everything… Is… Forty-two,” said Deep Thought, with infinite majesty and calm.
trail: The number reaches the public on radio first: Deep Thought gives its answer in “Fit the Fourth,” broadcast on BBC Radio 4 on 29 March 1978 ↗, with Geoffrey McGivern voicing the computer.
The novel follows: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, adapted from the first four radio fits, was published in London by Pan Books on 12 October 1979 ↗.
Wikiquote files the punchline under Chapter 27 ↗: “Forty-two,” said Deep Thought, with infinite majesty and calm.
Quote Investigator ↗ credits Adams, traces the scene to the 1978 radio programme, and quotes the novel passage from scans of the 1981 Pocket Books printing at pages 179–180.
source.excerptNote: The ellipses inside the speech are Adams’s own, marking Deep Thought’s pauses — not editorial cuts. The bracketed break stands for the intervening dialogue. Quote Investigator ↗ places the passage at pages 179–180 of the 1981 Pocket Books printing (1979 copyright), verified with scans.

author.name: Douglas Adams
author.heading: Who was Douglas Adams?
author.bio: Douglas Noël Adams was an English author, humourist and screenwriter who turned a late-night BBC Radio 4 comedy into one of the most quoted books in science fiction. The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy began as a 1978 radio series, became a novel in 1979, and grew into a “trilogy” of five books that sold more than 14 million copies in his lifetime; he also adapted it for television in 1981 and wrote a 1984 video game. He died in Santa Barbara, California, in 2001.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The line itself is real, and it has not been stolen from anyone. What travels is a smoothed-down version of it — plus a long tail of theories about where the number came from that Adams demolished himself.

items.why: Adams wrote the sentence with Deep Thought’s stately pauses built in: “The Answer to the Great Question… Of Life, the Universe and Everything… Is… Forty-two.” Reprints routinely close the gaps, and the still-shorter “the answer to life, the universe and everything is 42” is a summary rather than a line anyone speaks. Same sentence, stripped of its timing — Wikiquote files the punchline under Chapter 27 ↗.

items.who: “the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe and Everything”
items.why: Both phrases are in the book, but not in the same mouth. Deep Thought announces the answer to the Great Question; the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe and Everything is howled by Loonquawl in the following chapter ↗.

items.who: “What do you get if you multiply six by nine?”
items.why: The famously mismatched Question is not in the 1979 novel at all. It arrives at the end of The Restaurant at the End of the Universe (1980), when a Scrabble-playing caveman spells it out — “Six by nine. Forty two.” ↗

items.who: Lewis Carroll, Tibetan monks, base 13, binary 101010
items.why: Critics have pointed to 42 recurring throughout Lewis Carroll; fans have offered numerology, binary and base-13 arithmetic. Adams called them all nonsense: “I sat at my desk, stared into the garden and thought ‘42 will do’ I typed it out. End of story.” ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuine and it has not drifted: Douglas Adams wrote it for Deep Thought in Chapter 27 of the 1979 novel, after the answer first aired on BBC Radio 4 in March 1978 — and Quote Investigator verified the passage against scans ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Deep Thought is switched on to answer the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe and Everything, and warns its makers that this will take a while. Seven and a half million years later ↗ it delivers: forty-two. The joke was never the number. The joke is that nobody had worked out what the question was, so the answer is useless — which is why the story then needs a second, far larger computer, and why that computer turns out to be the Earth.

Adams spent the rest of his life being asked what 42 meant. Base 13, binary 101010, Tibetan monks, the angle at which light refracts to make a rainbow — he rejected the lot, in a post to the newsgroup alt.fan.douglas-adams dated 3 November 1993 ↗. Scientific American quotes him ↗ flatly: it was a joke, and the number simply had to be ordinary.
context.detailsSummary: The number Adams had already used once
detailsBody: 42 was not new to him. Adams had written a sketch for The Burkiss Way called “42 Logical Positivism Avenue,” broadcast on BBC Radio 4 on 12 January 1977 ↗ — before Hitchhiker’s put the number on air in “Fit the Fourth” on 29 March 1978.

In an interview with Iain Johnstone recorded in 1998 but never broadcast, Adams offered a longer account: he had worked as a prop-borrower for John Cleese on Video Arts training films, Cleese needed a funny number for a sketch punchline, and Adams believed the number Cleese landed on was 42 ↗. Stephen Fry, for his part, says Adams told him the real reason and that he has vowed to take it to his grave.
context.pull: It was a joke. It had to be a number, an ordinary, smallish number, and I chose that one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator credits Douglas Adams with originating the forty-two answer, traces the scene to the 1978 BBC radio programme, quotes the novel passage opening "All right," said Deep Thought. "The Answer to the Great Question . . .", and cites it at pages 179-180 of the 1981 Pocket Books printing (1979 copyright), verified with scans; it also cites The Original Hitchhiker Radio Scripts (1985, Harmony Books), Fit the Fourth, page 79, and Adams's "completely ordinary number" footnote at page 88.

Wikiquote lists under Chapter 27 the line "Forty-two," said Deep Thought, with infinite majesty and calm, annotated "The Answer to the Great Question, of Life, the Universe and Everything"; under Chapter 28 it records Loonquawl howling "But it was the Great Question! The Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe and Everything."
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy is a 1979 novel by Douglas Adams, adapted from the first four parts of his radio series, first published in London through Pan Books on 12 October 1979.

Deep Thought takes seven and a half million years to compute and check the answer; "42" was first broadcast in Fit the Fourth on 29 March 1978; Adams's sketch "42 Logical Positivism Avenue" for The Burkiss Way aired on BBC Radio 4 on 12 January 1977; on 3 November 1993 Adams posted to alt.fan.douglas-adams that "It was a joke... Binary representations, base thirteen, Tibetan monks are all complete nonsense. I sat at my desk, stared into the garden and thought '42 will do' I typed it out. End of story."; the six-by-nine Question comes from The Restaurant at the End of the Universe; Adams described his choice as "a completely ordinary number, a number not just divisible by two but also six and seven"; the John Cleese/Video Arts account comes from a 1998 Iain Johnstone interview recorded but never broadcast; Stephen Fry vowed to take the reason to his grave; some critics suggest Lewis Carroll influence.
Fit the Fourth was broadcast on BBC Radio 4 on 29 March 1978, with Deep Thought voiced by Geoffrey McGivern.

Douglas Noel Adams (11 March 1952 - 11 May 2001) was an English author, humourist and screenwriter; The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy originated in 1978 as a BBC radio comedy before developing into a trilogy of five books that sold more than 14 million copies in his lifetime, and he adapted it into a 1981 television series and a 1984 video game.

The Internet Archive holds a scan of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy by Douglas Adams (1952-2001), New York: Pocket Books, 1981, the record noting "First Pocket Books printing October, 1981" - the edition Quote Investigator cites.

The Internet Archive holds a scan of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy: the original radio scripts by Douglas Adams, London: Pan, 2003, with a catalog note that a previous edition was published as The Hitch-Hiker's Guide to the Galaxy, 1985.

Scientific American's "For Math Fans: A Hitchhiker's Guide to the Number 42" by Jean-Paul Delahaye (21 September 2020) quotes Adams verbatim: "It was a joke. It had to be a number, an ordinary, smallish number, and I chose that one," and reports he dismissed mathematical theories about the number as complete nonsense.
